Standard for Indirect Targeting
3.3.8.6 Employer’s Objective:
• The objective of the project is to provide a minimum Contract Participation Goal (CPG) of 30%
of the total project value and to develop targeted enterprises by the main or lead partner
contractors.
• The successful Contractor shall:
I. Subcontract a minimum of 5% of the total project value to targeted enterprises;
II. Develop the targeted enterprise/s in two development areas as specified in the Standard,
and agreed by both the Main Contractor and the targeted enterprise/s;
III. Perform needs analysis on the target enterprise to identify development goals;
IV. Provide internal mentorship support to improve the targeted enterprise/s performance,
V. Develop a project specific enterprise development plan to improve the targeted
enterprise/s performance in the identified development areas;
VI. Monitor and report the progress of the agreed development areas with the targeted
enterprise/s; and
VII. Submit a project completion report to the Employer’s Representative for each targeted
enterprise.
3.3.8.7 The development of the Targeted Enterprise shall be guided by the CIDB Competence Standard
for Contractors Gazette No. 41237, 10 November 2017. Table 2.
3.3.8.8 The Contractor shall appoint an Enterprise Development Coordinator who shall:
• Develop a project specific Enterprise Development Plan to improve the targeted enterprise’s
performance in the identified development areas and shall allocate resources to monitor
progress in relation to improved performance; and
• Shall submit to the Employer’s Representative a monthly enterprise development report
(Performa – ED105P) which documents all mentoring activities that have taken place during
that month, and the progress made in improving the targeted enterprise’s performance in the
agreed development areas, countersigned by the targeted enterprise.
3.3.8.9 Competence Criteria for an Enterprise Development Coordinator
The enterprise development coordinator shall have the following competencies:
a) Minimum experience of 5 years in the construction industry at Managerial level as a Site Agent,
Contracts Manager, Site Manager, Construction Manager, Business Development Manager or
Enterprise Development Manager.

5 Works Information
The Contractor shall be responsible for the design, supply, delivery, installation, configuration,
software integration, testing, and commissioning of all the AMR meters as well as the software
solution in all ports.
The scope to be carried out by the Contractor includes but not limited to the following items of work
as summarized below:
• Supply, install, configure, test and commission smart electricity meters for measurement of
different electrical parameters listed elsewhere in the document including Active Energy
(kWh/MWh), Reactive Energy (kVArh/MVArh), Apparent Energy (kVAh/MVAh) etc.
• Supply, install, configure, test and commission smart water meters for measurement of water
consumption (KL), alarm notification for high flow set points and trigger night flow analysis.
• Supply, installation and configuration of transmitters, data loggers/ recorder/ pulse and
counters.
• Design, develop, install, test and commission a smart utility management software solution
including all graphic displays, dashboards, tabs, report templates etc.
• Design, install, test and commission Fibre Optic Local Area Network and Private Wireless
Communication Network in each port.
• Selection of all communication and instrumentation required for Automatic Meter Reading (AMR)
including linking the meters to the billing servers.
• Billing Software: Create accounts, link them to the meters and setup the tariffs. The billing
software should also allow for capturing manual readings for Shipping water and small water
meters.
• Program and integrate the software solution to new and existing systems as well as the billing
servers.
• Link all the data servers from the eight ports to one central repository and allow retrieval of
information across the system.
• Testing and commissioning of the installations as individual and integrated system.
• Issuing of Valid calibration certificates, Data Books, Operating manuals, Maintenance plans and
schedules in both hard copy and electronic format.
• Supplying all necessary Materials, labour, tools, Plant, PPE, demarcating signage and transport
required for the proper Completion of the works.

COMMUNICATION INFRASTRUCTURE
5.1.6 Communication Infrastructure Requirements (LAN & Wireless Network)
5.1.6.1 Design a fibre optic Local Area Network within the port boundary.
5.1.6.2 Trench to lay the fibre optic sleeves, trenching to minimum depth of 600mm and a width of 300mm.
5.1.6.3 Supply and install 110mm PVC pipe and chamber system for the fibre.
5.1.6.4 Supply and install fibre optic manholes where required.
5.1.6.5 The trenching for complete installation shall not exceed a total length of 25km. Backfill and reinstate
existing surface and make good.
5.1.6.6 Supply and install 25 patch panels fully populated 48 pair with LC patch leads.
5.1.6.7 Supply, install and patch a total of 25km of 48 pair single mode fibre optic cable (652D).
5.1.6.8 Supply, install and configure 25 by 24 ports managed enterprise network switches.
5.1.6.9 Supply and install a 9U swing frame cabinet 900mm deep.
5.1.6.10 Link all electricity meters through the LAN to transmit data to the billing server for processing via
the Utilities Management Software.
5.1.7 Wireless Communication Network for the water meters
5.1.7.1 All waters are to be fitted with an AMR interface (IoT devices) for logging of data and communicate
to the closest gateway. The AMR interface shall have long range transmission and operate on low
power.
5.1.7.2 Supply and install metering gateways including civil and structural works and all appurtenances.
5.1.7.3 Configure and integrate the gateways onto the LAN to transfer data to the server and Utilities
Management Software.
5.1.7.4 Supply and install a server (Network & Application) to manage and control the network. The
network server shall receive data and control messages from the gateways and process the data.
The application server shall interface with the network server and shall store the data, perform
analytics and enable integration with other systems.
5.1.7.5 Develop an Application Programming Interface (API) to allow the network to transmit relevant
billing data to the billing server and Utilities Management Software.
5.1.8 Servers
5.1.8.1 Supply, install and configure two 8-core (2.10GHz), 16GB, 8 x Hot plug 2.5in, smart array P408ia,
2 x 500W, rack mount billing servers.
5.1.8.2 Each server shall be supplied with four 1.2TB Hard Drives.

EXISTING SYSTEMS AND INTEGRATION
5.3.3 The Contractor must develop an Application Programming Interface (APIs) to integrate the software
with existing systems including linking the Utility Management Software to Transnets’ Integrated
Port Management System (IPMS) and SAP ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) to transfer billing data
(kilo Liters & Rand Value, kilowatts hours & Rand Value) on 15th of each month.
COMMUNICATION INFRASTRUCTURE
5.3.4 Communication Infrastructure Requirements
5.3.4.1 Design a fibre optic Local Area Network within the port boundary.
5.3.4.2 Trench to lay the fibre optic sleeves, trenching to minimum depth of 600mm and a width of 300mm.
5.3.4.3 Supply and install 110mm PVC pipe and chamber system for the fibre.
Contract PAGE 52 Part C3
CPM 2020 Rev01 C3. Works Information

TRANSNET NATIONAL PORTS AUTHORITY
TENDER NUMBER: TNPA/2025/02/0002/89478/RFP
DESCRIPTION OF WORKS: SUPPLY AND INSTALLATION OF SMART WATER AND ELELCTRICITY METERS
WITH A SOFTWARE SOLUTION (UTILITIES MANAGEMENT) ACROSS THE EIGHT PORTS
5.3.4.4 Supply and install fibre optic manholes where required.
5.3.4.5 The trenching for complete installation shall not exceed a total length of 12km. Backfill and reinstate
existing surface and make good.
5.3.4.6 Supply and install 15 patch panels fully populated 48 pair with LC patch leads.
5.3.4.7 Supply, install and patch a total of 12km of 48 pair single mode fibre optic cable (652D).
5.3.4.8 Supply, install and configure 15 by 24 ports managed enterprise network switches.
5.3.4.9 Supply and install a 9U swing frame cabinet 900mm deep.
5.3.4.10 Link all electricity meters through the LAN to transmit data to the billing server for processing via
the Utilities Management Software.
5.3.5 Wireless Communication Network for the water meters
5.3.5.1 All waters are to be fitted with an AMR interface (IoT devices) for logging of data and communicate
to the closest gateway. The AMR interface shall have long range transmission and operate on low
power.
5.3.5.2 Supply and install metering gateways including civil and structural works and all appurtenances.
5.3.5.3 Configure and integrate the gateways onto the LAN to transfer data to the server and Utilities
Management Software.
5.3.5.4 Supply and install a server (Network & Application) to manage and control the network. The
network server shall receive data and control messages from the gateways and process the data.
The application server shall interface with the network server and shall store the data, perform
analytics and enable integration with other systems.
5.3.5.5 Develop an Application Programming Interface (API) to allow the network to transmit relevant
billing data to the billing server and Utilities Management Software.
5.3.6 Server
5.3.6.1 Supply, install and configure two 8-core (2.10GHz), 16GB, 8 x Hot plug 2.5in, smart array P408ia,
2 x 500W, rack mount billing servers.
5.3.6.2 Each server shall be supplied with four 1.2TB Hard Drives.
5.3.6.3 Supply and install the latest Microsoft SQL server (permanent license) for the management of data,
storage and perform analytics via the Utilities Management Software.
5.3.7 Firewall
5.3.7.1 Supply, install, configure, and commission a Firewall for LAN. The Contractor shall ensure that old
and new services going through the Firewall are reinstated.
5.3.7.2 Setup DMZ and position a management workstation within DMZ.

Site Conditions
All Plants and Materials offered shall be rated for continuous operation under the following service
conditions: (Port to inputs data)
Altitude Sea level to +50m
Ambient air temperature Max. 40 degrees Celsius; Min. – 5 degrees Celsius
Humidity As high as 86%
Lightning conditions 10 strikes per year as listed in SABS codes
Atmosphere Highly saline with heavy corrosive industrial, chemical and dust-
laden nature. Frequent heavy rains driven by winds reaching speeds
of 100km/h and above.
Water supply pressure between 2.0 – 6.0bar

5.6.2 New Below Ground Water Meter Installation
The Contractor shall perform the following activities for the 29 new proposed below ground meter
installations:
5.6.2.1 Proof trench and verify the pipe material, depth and pipe size before procuring any material for the
installation.
5.6.2.2 The existing pipe material is UPVC and the pipe size ranges from 110mm to 160mm.
5.6.2.3 Saw cut approximately 4.7x1m wide in 50mm premix and hack up and remove including layer
works and re-instate to match existing once all work is complete.
5.6.2.4 Excavate in earth in varying depths but not exceeding 1.5m deep, approximately 4.7x1m wide to
expose existing water pipe including all necessary risk of collapse, backfilling and compaction and
cart away of surplus material from site.
5.6.2.5 Cutting off approximately 4.5m of pipe including fitting of flanges on both ends of exposed pipe.
5.6.2.6 Construct a new water meter manhole with overall size 2.66x1.66m and varying depths not
exceeding 2.53m deep including all necessary additional excavations, risk of collapse, blinding,
manhole base, stone bedding, 230mm brickwork, backfilling, concrete cover slab, including
breaking openings on both ends for new pipe and cart away of surplus material all in accordance
with drawings and specifications.
5.6.2.7 Supply and install No. 02x steel pipes each approximately 1.4m in length, flanged on both ends
and fitted on either end of manhole to existing pipes and in new manholes including sealing off
ends of manholes, support/thrust blocks, etc., gaskets, bolts, sealants etc.
5.6.2.8 Supply and install No. 02x spool pieces in varying lengths flanged on both ends and fixed to meter
& valves including all necessary, gaskets, bolts, sealants etc.
5.6.2.9 Supply and install a swing check valve flanged on both ends and fixed to new-flanged pipes
including all necessary gaskets, bolts, sealants etc.
5.6.2.10 Supply and install an In-line strainer, flanged on both ends and fixed to new-flanged pipes including
all necessary gaskets, bolts, sealants etc.

Site Conditions
All Plants and Materials offered shall be rated for continuous operation under the following service
conditions: (Port to inputs data)
Altitude Sea level to +50m
Ambient air temperature Max. 40 degrees Celsius; Min. – 5 degrees Celsius
Humidity As high as 86%
Lightning conditions 10 strikes per year as listed in SABS codes
Atmosphere Highly saline with heavy corrosive industrial, chemical and dust-
laden nature. Frequent heavy rains driven by winds reaching speeds
of 100km/h and above.
Water supply pressure between 2.0 – 6.0bar

COMMUNICATION INFRASTRUCTURE
5.7.10 Communication Infrastructure Requirements
5.7.10.1 Design a fibre optic Local Area Network within the port boundary.
5.7.10.2 Trench to lay the fibre optic sleeves, trenching to minimum depth of 600mm and a width of
300mm.
5.7.10.3 Supply and install 110mm PVC pipe and chamber system for the fibre.
5.7.10.4 Supply and install fibre optic manholes where required.
5.7.10.5 The trenching for complete installation shall not exceed a total length of 13km. Backfill and
reinstate existing surface and make good.
5.7.10.6 Supply and install 15 patch panels fully populated 48 pair with LC patch leads.
5.7.10.7 Supply, install and patch a total of 13km of 48 pair single mode fibre optic cable (652D).
5.7.10.8 Supply, install and configure 15 by 24 ports managed enterprise network switches.
5.7.10.9 Supply and install a 9U swing frame cabinet 900mm deep.
5.7.10.10 Link all electricity meters through the LAN to transmit data to the billing server for processing via
the Utilities Management Software.
5.7.11 Wireless Communication Network for the water meters
5.7.11.1 All waters are to be fitted with an AMR interface (IoT devices) for logging of data and
communicate to the closest gateway. The AMR interface shall have long range transmission and
operate on low power.
5.7.11.2 Supply and install metering gateways including civil and structural works and all appurtenances.
5.7.11.3 Configure and integrate the gateways onto the LAN to transfer data to the server and Utilities
Management Software.
5.7.11.4 Supply and install a server (Network & Application) to manage and control the network. The
network server shall receive data and control messages from the gateways and process the data.
The application server shall interface with the network server and shall store the data, perform
analytics and enable integration with other systems.
5.7.11.5 Develop an Application Programming Interface (API) to allow the network to transmit relevant
billing data to the billing server and Utilities Management Software.
5.7.12 Server
5.7.12.1 Supply, install and configure two 8-core (2.10GHz), 16GB, 8 x Hot plug 2.5in, smart array P408ia,
2 x 500W, rack mount billing servers.

Site Conditions
All Plants and Materials offered shall be rated for continuous operation under the following service
conditions: (Port to inputs data)
Altitude Sea level to +50m
Ambient air temperature Max. 40 degrees Celsius; Min. – 5 degrees Celsius
Humidity As high as 86%
Lightning conditions 10 strikes per year as listed in SABS codes
Atmosphere Highly saline with heavy corrosive industrial, chemical and dust-
laden nature. Frequent heavy rains driven by winds reaching speeds
of 100km/h and above.
Water supply pressure between 2.0 – 6.0bar

TRANSNET NATIONAL PORTS AUTHORITY
TENDER NUMBER: TNPA/2025/02/0002/89478/RFP
DESCRIPTION OF WORKS: SUPPLY AND INSTALLATION OF SMART WATER AND ELELCTRICITY METERS
WITH A SOFTWARE SOLUTION (UTILITIES MANAGEMENT) ACROSS THE EIGHT PORTS
EXISTING SYSTEMS AND INTEGRATION
5.8.24 The Contractor must develop an Application Programming Interface (APIs) to integrate the
software with existing systems including linking the Utility Management Software to Transnets’
Integrated Port Management System (IPMS) and SAP ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) to
transfer billing data (kilo Liters & Rand Value, kilowatts hours & Rand Value) on 15th of each month.
COMMUNICATION INFRASTRUCTURE
5.8.25 Communication Infrastructure Requirements
5.8.25.1 Design a fibre optic Local Area Network within the port boundary.
5.8.25.2 Trench to lay the fibre optic sleeves, trenching to minimum depth of 600mm and a width of
300mm.
5.8.25.3 Supply and install 110mm PVC pipe and chamber system for the fibre.
5.8.25.4 Supply and install fibre optic manholes where required.
5.8.25.5 The trenching for complete installation shall not exceed a total length of 10km. Backfill and
reinstate existing surface and make good.
5.8.25.6 Supply and install 10 patch panels fully populated 48 pair with LC patch leads
5.8.25.7 Supply, install and patch a total of 10km of 48 pair single mode fibre optic cable.
5.8.25.8 Supply, install and configure 10 by 24 ports managed enterprise network switches.
5.8.25.9 Supply and install a 9U swing frame cabinet 900mm deep.
5.8.25.10 Link all electricity meters through the LAN to transmit data to the billing server for processing via
the Utilities Management Software.
5.8.26 Wireless Communication Network for the water meters
5.8.26.1 All waters are to be fitted with an AMR interface (IoT devices) for logging of data and
communicate to the closest gateway. The AMR interface shall have long range transmission and
operate on low power.
5.8.26.2 Supply and install metering gateways including civil and structural works and all appurtenances.
5.8.26.3 Configure and integrate the gateways onto the LAN to transfer data to the server and Utilities
Management Software.
5.8.26.4 Supply and install a server (Network & Application) to manage and control the network. The
network server shall receive data and control messages from the gateways and process the data.
The application server shall interface with the network server and shall store the data, perform
analytics and enable integration with other systems.
5.8.26.5 Develop an Application Programming Interface (API) to allow the network to transmit relevant
billing data to the billing server and Utilities Management Software.

5.10 Advance Metering Infrastructure (AMI)
This section covers the requirements for the Automated Meter Reading (AMR) technology to be
used in collecting water consumption on the water reticulation network installed in each port. AMR
devices will collect and transmit the water meter data directly to Gateways that will then route it
further via the TNPA Engineering Local Area Network (LAN) to the billing server in the port. All
devices must be covered by at least 2 to 3 gateways that can read data from that device, the
devices shall have a redundancy factor of 2.

5.10.1 Private Long Range Wireless Area Network
5.10.1.1 The Contractor shall investigate, design and install a private wireless communication network that
will allow reading of the water meters remotely and transmit the water meter data via Gateways
that will then route the data further via the TNPA Engineering Local Area Network (LAN) to the
billing server in the port and upload the data into the new Utility Management System using
Microsoft enterprise SQL server database.
5.10.1.2 The wireless network shall have long-range communication (up to 10km), ultra low power and
deep indoor penetration.
5.10.1.3 Each gateway/ receiver shall have the capability to support up to 1000 devices/ meters.
5.10.1.4 The wireless communication network solution shall be robust and secure ICASA approved open
non-proprietary radio frequency protocols which optimize and enhance communication range and
lengthen battery life meters (built-in radio), meter interface units and gateways shall be preferred.
5.10.1.5 The wireless communication system shall seamlessly integrate with existing systems in the ports.
The AMR solution shall communicate via an open protocol such as TCP/IP, Modbus etc.
5.10.1.6 Gateways are to be linked back to the servers via the Local Area Network.
5.10.1.7 The wireless network shall be easy to install, manage and maintain.
5.10.1.8 The network system shall have the capabilities to be monitored via a dashboard and have the
ability to trace the water data back through the system to the meter. Timestamps should reflect
when the meter took its reading and where the data was held. Each reading should be uniquely
tied to the meter it came from to avoid the possibility of confusion.
5.10.1.9 If communication fails for a period (failed batteries, network outage/congestion), the system
should be able to retrieve missed data from the meter itself. In addition, the system shall allow
for a handheld (Drive by or Walk by) device to be used to pick-up data or collect meter readings
should any communication failure occur.
5.10.1.10 The communication network shall operate on a license free spectrum (No ICASA License).
5.10.1.11 The wireless network solution shall have no monthly or yearly subscriptions. Cloud solutions
will not be considered.
5.10.2 AMR Gateways and Communication
5.10.2.1 Gateways are to be used to collect data from the meters and upload to the billing server via the
LAN network. The gateways shall be easy to install and configure and shall be compatible with
LoRa, Wi-Fi, Fiber (RTU), Ethernet and GSM/GRPS/LTE.
5.10.2.2 The Gateway shall communicate in the unlicensed managed 868 MHz range with all the AMR
modules in its assigned area and must be capable to cover up to 8 km radius.
5.10.2.3 The gateway data collectors shall collect data from the devices and send the data to the billing
server. The transmission interval shall be adjustable between 30 minutes to 24 hours.

5.10.2.5 The gateways shall be configurable via fixed IP address for on the Local Area Network.

5.10.2.7 The gateways shall be PoE (Power over Ethernet) or AC or solar powered unit with optional

5.10.3 Automatic Meter Reading (AMR) Interface
5.10.3.1 The meter interface shall be Hall Effect sensors, reed switches are to be avoided due to their
mechanical nature and the danger of physical break.
5.10.3.2 The meter interface shall have a communication range of up to 10km open environment and at
least 5km range urban and must be compatible with Wi-Fi, Fibre (RTU), Ethernet and
GSM/GRPS/LTE connection.
5.10.3.3 The interface shall be LoRa certified.
5.10.3.4 The device shall be powered by a battery and it shall be replaceable and serviceable batteries.
The battery life shall be between 5 to 10 years or more. (extended battery pack)
5.10.3.5 The AMR interface shall be capable to give the following:
o Meter ID
o Meter Address
o Meter Reading in (kL)
o Meter Reading Date
o Low Battery Alert
o High Flow Alert
o Low Flow Alert
o Tamper Alert
o Meter Error Alert
o Back Flow Alert

ring configuration at each port that will interconnect various devices (i.e., Electricity Meters, AMR
Gateways, Servers and Management Workstation). The fiber optic installation shall be carried out
in accordance with “Annexure E: Project Specification Fiber Cable 08-2025”. The fiber network shall
have core redundancy in the following areas:

5.12 Smart Utility Management Software Solution
This section covers the requirements for the utility management software to be deployed at each
port for managing both water and electricity consumption within the port. The data collected from
the meters will be stored in the servers using SQL server database. The stored data will be
analysed on the server and available for display via the Utility Management Software Solution
graphical user interface (Dashboards). No cloud-based solutions will be accepted.
5.12.1 Development of Smart Utility Management Software Solution
5.12.1.1 Development, installation, testing and commissioning of a smart utility management software
solution. The software solution to be developed shall be able to retrieve water and electricity data
from various software and be able to monitor, perform analysis and store TNPA’s metering data.

5.13 Technical specification of the Water Meter
5.13.1 Water Meter:
5.13.1.1 All meters are to be SANS 1529-1:2006 as well as Trade Metrology Act, 1973 (Act 77 of 1973)
compliant.
5.13.1.2 The meter shall comprise of a 9-digit analog display for consumption (m3) and status
information.
5.13.1.3 Have a built-in radio AMR capabilities.
5.13.1.4 The meter shall have a dial compatible with a High Resolution Interface (HRI)
5.13.1.5 Detect continuous water leaks.
5.13.1.6 Offer two communication modes, fixed radio network and mobile read (Walk-by/ Drive-by)
5.13.1.7 Protection Class IP68
5.13.1.8 Maximum working pressure 1600kPa
5.13.1.9 In all cases, the tenderer shall give a full description of the meter offered. Corrosion resistant
materials shall be employed throughout and parts that are in contact with the water flowing
through shall be non-toxic and non-tainting.
5.13.1.10 The meter body must be manufactured from cast iron and powder coated with a fusion bonded
epoxy to a minimum dry thickness of 150 microns.
5.13.1.11 Meter installation position shall be horizontal.
5.13.1.12 The water meter shall be clearly and indelibly marked with the following information:
a) Name or trademark of the manufacturer.
b) Meter serial number where first two digits indicate year of
manufacture.
c) Direction of flow on both sides of the body
d) Unit of measurement
e) Meter type and size
f) Maximum admissible pressure
g) Pressure loss class

5.14.1 Electricity Meter
All smart electricity meters supplied shall have the capabilities to measure different electrical
parameters such as but not limited to Active Energy (kWh/MWh), Reactive Energy
(kVArh/MVArh), Apparent Energy (kVAh/MVAh) etc. in a three (3) phase, three or four wire 50
Hz network.
Specification of the meter:
• Frequency: 50Hz ± 2%
• Accuracy: Class 0.5S Active Energy (kWh), Class 1.0 Reactive Energy (kVArh)
• Voltage 3 x 58/100...240/415V
• Current: 1/5A
• Maximum continuous current: 200% In
• Other data: Instantaneous values
• Switching: Internal clock
• Outputs: 5 Input, 6 outputs contacts
• Standard: IEC 60687 & IEC 61035
• Data output: LCD,
Meter construction
• Display: Programmable 8-digit liquid crystal display and shall be capable to display while un-
powered.
• Figure height: 8mm
• Construction: Anti static, glass fibre re-enforced plastic
Communication
The meter must be compatible with Wi-Fi, Fibre, Ethernet and GSM/GRPS/LTE connection.

7.3.14 Asbestos that forms part of structure of building or on premises
7.3.12.1 Handling of Asbestos Cement Products
In order to ensure that the handling, altering, cleaning, preparation for painting or removal of
any asbestos cement products, is carried out in a safe, uniform and appropriate manner as
required by the Asbestos Abatement Regulations 2020, framed under the Occupational Health
and Safety Act (Act No. 85 of 1993) and the Environment Conservation Act, 1989 (Act No 73 of
1989), the Contractor will either:
a) Acquire the services of an Asbestos Approved Inspection Authority in order to train their
employees and draw up Plan of Work. It must comply with requirements of Regulation 15;
b) Acquire the services of a Registered Asbestos Removal Contractor. The services of the
AAIA must be acquired by the awarded Contractor for the project;
c) Keep all records on the SHE File relating to asbestos management on site and that includes
proof of training, air monitoring results, etc. which will be handed over to the TNPA Project
Leader upon completion of the work / contract;
d) Provide an up-to-date inventory of asbestos in place, as contemplated in regulation 4, when
asbestos work is planned;
e) Ensure that an asbestos risk assessment, as contemplated in regulation 5, is carried out prior
to asbestos work;
f) Ensure that a written safe work procedure is developed and followed by employees.
7.3.12.2 Disposal of Asbestos Cement Products
The Contractor shall ensure that all Asbestos Cement Products are disposed at an Asbestos
disposal site (approved for disposal of hazardous material) that means a site specifically
designated for the purpose of asbestos disposal in terms of the National Environmental
Management: Waste Act, 2008 (Act No. 59 of 2008).

7.4 Environmental constraints and management
The Contractor complies with the following Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP):
7.4.1 The Contractor performs the works and all construction activities within the Site and Working Areas
in accordance with the provisions of the environmental management plan guidelines as contained
in the Employer’s Standard Environmental Specifications.
7.4.2 The Contractor performs the works and all construction activities within the Site and Working Areas
having due regard to the environment and to environmental management practices as more
particularly described within the Standard Environmental Specification (SES) and Project
Environmental Specifications (PES).
7.4.3 The SES describes the minimal acceptable standard for environmental management for a range of
environmental aspects commonly encountered on construction projects and sets environmental
objectives and targets, which the Contractor observes and complies.
7.4.4 The PES describes more particularly the environmental standards applicable to the works, the Site
and the Working Areas and sets out variance (including additions) to the SES. The PES may require
higher minimal standards than those described in the SES as may be required by the Project
Manager or Others.
7.4.5 The overarching obligations of the Contractor under the CEMP before construction activities
commence on the Site and/or Working Areas is to provide an environmental method statement for
a particular construction operation at the Site and/or Working Area by the Contractor and where
requested by the CM and to comply with the following:
The Contractor shall identify the kinds of environmental impacts that will occur as a result of his
activities and a method statement describing how each of those impacts will be avoided, prevented
or managed so that the standards set out in this documents are achieved.
The EMP must include, but not limited to the following sections detailing the environmental aspects
and possible impacts and management controls (mitigation measures) pertaining to the risks listed
in the section:
• Site establishment including Contractor’s Site camp
• Protection of sensitive/no-go areas
• Management of hazardous chemicals and flammable substances
• Pollution control & Spill response
• Waste Management
• Environmental education and awareness
• Protection of marine species and birds
• Removal of project waste

This document contains the engineering and construction activities for all eight ports. The ports
have been organized into three main regions: Eastern, Central and Western, each with its own
distinct characteristics and specialized services. The Eastern region includes Durban and Richards
Bay. The Central region consists of East London, Ngqura and Port Elizabeth. The Western region
is composed of Mossel Bay, Cape Town and Saldanha.
The Contractor is required to have construction/ installation Teams per region (Eastern, Central
and Western) and the Teams are to be subdivided into two i.e., one for the supply and installation
of water meters and one for the supply and installation of electricity meters. These installations
shall take place simultaneously. The Contractor is required to provide all necessary resources, tools
and equipment to support this strategy. These requirements shall be included in the Contractor’s
schedule by the Contractor.

1. BACKGROUND
An important element of protecting the Transnet resources is controlling and managing the
ability of users to access and modify resources and the information stored within them.
Therefore, user management gives Transnet the ability to control, monitor and protect
information resources availability, integrity, and confidentiality.
Operational Technology (OT) involves hardware and software that directly monitor and control
physical devices and processes. As OT systems integrate more with IT, they become
vulnerable to cyber threats, requiring stricter security measures. This OT Standard aims to
establish consistent guidelines and controls for protecting OT environments, ensuring secure
and reliable operations. It supports best practices to safeguard OT systems, mitigate risks,
and ensure regulatory compliance within our IT infrastructure.
1. PURPOSE
The purpose of this document is to identify and monitor the controls associated with the
Operational Technology (OT) or Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) or OT
efficiency, and sustainability of core operational controls, as part of the annual Internal Audit
Plan, TIA will perform audit testing to ensure compliance with the OT controls. This will further
strengthen the management and execution of the control activities within the OT environment.
This

which in turn supports the ICT Governance Policy and ICT Governance Framework as

1. DEFINITION & ABBREVIATIONS
For ease of reference words, expressions and abbreviations used in the standard are defined
below:
BUE: Business Unit Executive A senior manager responsible for the operational and
strategic management of a specific business unit within the organization.
CCTV: Closed-Circuit Television A security camera system used for monitoring and
surveillance of physical areas to ensure safety.
DBA: Database Administrator An IT professional responsible for installing, maintaining,
and securing database systems to ensure data integrity and performance.
DMZ: Demilitarized Zone A network segment that acts as a buffer between an internal
network and external networks (such as the internet) to enhance security.
IDS: Intrusion Detection System A security solution that monitors network traffic for
suspicious activities and potential cyber threats, alerting administrators of any detected
anomalies.
IPS: Intrusion Prevention System A security system that not only detects but also actively
blocks or mitigates potential cyber threats to prevent unauthorized access and attacks.
OT: Operational Technology Control systems used to manage industrial processes,
including SCADA systems, PLCs, and other industrial control devices.
PCITR: OT Incident Response Team A specialized team responsible for handling and
mitigating cybersecurity incidents related to operational technology.
PLC: Programmable Logic Controller A ruggedized industrial computer used for
automation and control of machinery and processes in manufacturing and infrastructure
systems.
Process Control: The use of automated control systems, including PLCs and SCADA, to
monitor and manage industrial processes to ensure efficiency, safety, and reliability.
6 of 23
© Transnet SOC Ltd,

SCADA: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition A system used for remote monitoring
and control of industrial processes, such as power plants, water treatment facilities, and
manufacturing operations.
SOP: Standard Operating Procedures A set of step-by-step instructions designed to ensure
consistent and efficient execution of processes within an organization.
TIA: Transnet Internal Audit The internal auditing division of Transnet responsible for
evaluating financial, operational, and compliance risks within the organization.
TCP/IP: Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol A fundamental set of
networking protocols that enable communication over the internet and other networks.
RTU: Remote Terminal Unit A field device used in SCADA systems to collect data from
sensors and send control signals to connected equipment.
1. ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
5.1. ICT Architecture Review Council
Responsible for the approval of all Transnet ICT standards.

Responsible to manage and co-ordinate Transnet Group ICT risk mitigation and
governance activities across the Group and to co-ordinate activities regarding the
recommending Transnet ICT standards to the ICT Architecture Review Council.
Participate in the development and maintenance of the standard and the related
procedures.
5.3. GM: GICT Governance, Risk and Security
Owner of this standard.
Reviews and supports waivers that have been compiled for exception from
compliance with this standard.
Provide strategic direction, resources, and oversight for OT security initiatives.
Approve policies, allocate resources, monitor compliance, and review risk assessment
reports to support OT security and compliance.
5.4. Operating Division Information Security Liaison
Facilitate the implementation of the standard in the OD by communicating the
requirements, providing technical assistance with implementation, and reporting
adherence to the standard.
Collaborate with OT personnel to implement and enforce security measures across IT
and OT systems.
Perform joint security assessments, monitor for cyber threats, and assist in
developing incident response protocols specific to OT systems.
Ensure OT processes comply with internal policies and regulations.
Conduct compliance reviews, report compliance status, and provide recommendations
to align OT practices with regulatory requirements.

6.28. Data Protection and Privacy
Objective: To ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and security of sensitive
information within the OT environment, the following protection measures must be
implemented:
Requirements Frequency
6.28.1. Protection of Personal Information Once off /
(i) Where personal information is processed, adequate Ongoing
protection measures must be in place to prevent unauthorized
access, modification, or disclosure as per the requirements of
the Protection of Personal Information Act.
(ii)Access to personal information must be restricted to
authorized personnel using role-based access controls (RBAC)
or equivalent security mechanisms.
(iii)Encryption and secure storage must be applied where
feasible to protect personal data at rest and in transit.
(v)Logging and monitoring must be enabled to detect and
respond to unauthorized access or misuse of personal
information.
6.28.2. Protection of Data-in-Transit Once Off
(i) Critical data-in-transit must be encrypted as per the
requirements of the Transnet ICT Cryptography Standard.
(ii) Communication channels between OT devices, control
systems, and external networks must be secured to protect
sensitive operational data.
(iii) Network segmentation must be implemented to separate
critical OT traffic from less secure IT and external networks.
(iv) Remote access to OT systems must be secured using VPNs,
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), and encrypted sessions to
prevent unauthorized access.
1. EXCEPTIONS
The OT Standard has been developed to ensure a consistent approach across Transnet ICT
divisions for minimizing security risks and effectively managing OT environments. Any
exemptions from compliance with this standard must be approved by the ISGRC Committee
and accompanied by a comprehensive risk analysis and mitigating controls. This analysis
must outline the specific circumstances that prevent full implementation of the standard and
detail the compensating controls established to address any resulting risks.

SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 2 of 15

1. SCOPE
This specification cover Transnet National Port Authority requirements for handling,
installation, termination, joints and testing for cabling networks that use fiber optic
cables and related components to carry signals for communications.
1. BACKBONE LAN CABLE TYPE
This Tender calls for the installation testing and commissioning of 48 core long span
single mode fiber optical 1310nm network (LAN) for the following Ports:
a) Richard Bay
b) East London
c) Ngqura
d) Port Elizabeth
e) Mossel Bay
f) Cape Town
g) Saldanha
The Contractor shall establish a backbone network with redundant ring at each port that
interconnects various devices. The network should act as the central pathway for data
exchange and provide a reliable and high-speed connection between the various
devices.
Special requirements:
• Installing full drum lengths of cables without any splicing joints in cable length
except if joint is to connect to new full drum length “drum length shall be
deemed to be 5000m per drum”
• Fiber cable installation in ground:
o Where cable is installed next to the Ports security fence concrete coulomb
in ground it will be placed 500mm below ground level and inside an inner
orange thick wall blow tube pipe, that will be placed inside a 110mm
perverted pipe.
o Pipe will be laid in a 6mm dia max sifted bedding of excavated trench
sand 100 thick on base and 100mm above pipe above the pipe
o Above this last layer of sifted sand danger tape will be installed and then
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 3 of 15

trench can be back filled
o Compaction of excavation will be done in 150 mm layers
o No stone of object larger than ½ coronation brick will be used in backfill
material this will form part of the soil removal quantity
o Manhole to manhole will be maxim 500M
o All 90 deg bends or direction change will be done in Manholes
o No Manholes will be installed with in 1 meter of any road or driveway
o After compaction all material and execs sand rubble will be removed from
site.
In each manhole at least 5 full coils of cable shall be left for maintenance/repairs in
future if required.
1. INSTALLING FIBER OPTIC CABLE
3.1. Follow the cable manufacturer’s recommendations for installing the fiber optic cable.
The manufacturer may have specific instructions on its installations.
3.2. Check the cable length to make sure the cable being pulled is long enough for the run to
prevent having to splice fiber and provide special protection for the splices.
3.3. Try to complete the installation in one pull. Prior to any installatiuon, assess the route
carefully to determine the methods of installation and obstacles likely to be
encountered.
3.4. Never directly pull on the fiber itself. Fiber optic cables have aramid yarn for pulling.
Fiber optic cable should only be pulled by these strength members. Any other method
may put stress on the fibers and harm them.
3.5. Swivel pulling eyes should be used to attach the pulling rope or tape to the cable to
prevent cable twisting during the pull.
3.6. Do not exceed the maximum pulling load/tension rating. On long runs pulled in conduit,
it may be necessary to use lubricants. Make certain they are compatible with the cable
jacket. If possible, use an automated puller with tension control and/or a breakaway
pulling eye. On very long runs, pull from the middle out to both ends or use an
automated fiber puller at intermediate points for a continuous pull. Know and observe
the maximum recommended load rating of the cable manufacture data sheets.
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 4 of 15

Figure 1: Automated puller with tension control
Bend Radius
3.7. Do not exceed the cable bend radius. Fiber optic cable can be broken when kinked
or bent too tightly, especially during pulling. Fiber is stronger than steel when you
pull it straight, but it breaks easily when bent too tightly. These will harm the fibers,
maybe immediately, maybe not for a few years, but you will harm them and the
cable must be removed and thrown away.
3.8. If no specific recommendations are available from the cable manufacturer, the cable
should not be pulled over a bend radius smaller than twenty (20) times the cable
diameter.
3.9. After completion of the pull, the cable should not have any bend radius smaller than
ten (10) times the cable diameter.
Figure 2: Cable bend radius illustration
3.10. Always roll the cable off the spool instead of spinning it off the spool end. This will
put a twist in the cable for every turn on the spool! Never twist the fiber cable.
Putting a twist in the cable can stress the fibers.
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 5 of 15

Figure 3: Roller cable off the spool to prevent twisting
3.11. Pull, do not push cables. Pushing can result in violation of the bend radius, Monitor
the supply reel. Monitoring the supply reel during installation is necessary to prevent
violation of minimum bend radius.
Figure 4: Roller cable off the spool to prevent twisting
3.12. Communicate along the path of installation. When installing long runs, communicate
and monitor along the path of the installation. Fiber cables can and do jump from
unmonitored pulleys. The minimum crew should have one person monitoring the
pulling equipment, one monitoring the supply reel, and one coordinating all involved
in the installation.
3.13. Plan the Installation. Create a detailed, written plan of installation. You can eliminate
95% of the problems installers can encounter by simply creating this plan. The plan
should include equipment and supplies, fiber cable specification, location of
equipment, testing requirements, data forms for testing, personnel experience level
and assignment, installation methods, identification of potential obstructions.
3.14. Use fiber optic cable lubricant. Lubricate the cable when installing in conduits.
Lubrication reduces the pulling load and the chance of breakage. The lubricant has
to be compatible with the cable jacket material.
3.15. Use the figure 8 technique. Divide long pulls into several shorter pulls, using “figure
8” technique for storing cable at the intermediate locations. The cable is placed on
the ground in a figure 8 pattern. This pattern is large, at least 10-20 feet from top to
bottom of the pattern. When all the cable is placed in this pattern, the pattern is
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 6 of 15

lifted and flipped over, so that the loose end is on top. This loose end is pulling into
the ext section of conduit or duct. This technique prevents twisting in the cable.
Figure 5: Use “figure 8” loops to protect the cable when pulling
3.16. Comply with vertical rise limits. Know and observe the maximum vertical rise
distance limit. Exceeding this limit can result in fiber breakage, excess attenuation,
and, in loose tube cables, fibers sliding from cables. Cables in vertical installations
that are longer than the vertical rise limit must be tied off at distances less than this
limit. Loose tube cables must be looped.
3.17. Allow for thermal expansion and contraction. In outdoor installations, a common
practice of 2.5 foot sag for 150 foot span is good for thermal expansion and
contraction. Failure to allow for thermal expansion can result in increased
attenuation and breakage of fibers
3.18. For tough installations, use loose buffer tube fiber cables. Loose tube cables can be
more forgiving of abuse than tight buffer cables. The reason is that the excess
length of fiber in the buffer tube and the ability of fiber to move from low stress
region to higher stress region
3.19. Observe the temperature operating range. Install a cable in locations in which the
temperature range imposed is within the temperature operating range. Violation of
the temperature operating range can result in excessively high attenuation
3.20. Cap or seal water blocked cables. Cap off or seal the ends of cables with water
blocking gel or grease. These materials can flow out of the cable, causing
maintenance problems in cable end boxes
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 7 of 15

3.21. Protect fibers and buffer tubes. Confine fibers and buffer tubes in protective
structures, such as splice trays and cable end boxes. Fibers and buffer tubes do not
have sufficient strength to resist breakage due to normal handling of copper cables.
3.22. Loop vertically installed loose tube cables. Install vertical, unfilled, loose tube cables
with loops to prevent the fiber from slipping to the bottom of a vertical run. If this
happens, attenuation can increase, and fibers eventually break.
3.23. Check continuity and attenuation. Check the continuity and attenuation of the cable
before each operation. These checks should be performed as-received/before
installation, after installation, after splicing, and after connector installation.
3.24. Mark cable as “TNPA Electrical Fiber Optic Cable”. Mark cable as “TNPA Electrical
Fiber Optic Cable” in all locations in which it can be easily reached. Such marking will
alert electricians to the nature of the cable and identification.
3.25. Make As-Built Data files per substation. Keep this data available to those who will
perform maintenance and troubleshooting. These data logs should include both
insertion loss measurement and OTDR measurements.
3.26. Leave service loops. Leave cable and fiber service loops everywhere. You will regret
not doing so. Service loops allow you to pull excess cable or fiber into a location
where you have experienced a problem. It is much cheaper to pull in a service loop
than to replace an entire run of fiber cable. A small amount of slack cable (20-30
feet) can be useful in the event that cable repair or relocation is needed
3.27. Safety precaution – no food, drink or smoke. Do not eat, drink, or smoke in any area
in which bare glass fiber is created. Bare glass fibers can cause splinters which are
very difficult to find and remove.
3.28. Safety precaution – do not look into fiber without checking status. Never look into a
fiber cable or connector unless you know for sure that there is no laser light in the
fiber. For extensive work with fiber optics, safety glasses with IR filter is
recommended.
3.29. Segregate or isolate the work area. Rope off or otherwise isolate the area of cable
installation to prevent access to unauthorized or untrained personnel. This will avoid
safety problems such as fiber splinters and unintentional abuse.
3.30. For direct burial installations, the cable should lie flat in a trench, free of any large
stones or boulders that may deform the cable.
3.31. Avoid placing cable reels on their sides or subjecting them to shock from dropping.
3.32. Ensure that the proper cable length has been installed before cutting off excess
cable.
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 8 of 15

3.33. After the fiber optic cable is installed into a duct or innerduct, end plugs should be
installed to provide an effective water seal. The ducts and inner ducts should be kept
free of debris and maintained watertight at all times.
3.34. Ducts and inner ducts should be sized to meet present and future cable installation
requirements. A maximum 40% fill ratio is a good rule of thumb to follow for duct
size.
3.35. The fiber pulling rope or tape should be sequentially marked (foot or meter) for easy
identification of distance.
3.36. The pulling tape should have a rating for greater than maximum anticipated pulling
tension.
3.37. Before the start of any cable pull, all ducts and cable vaults should be carefully
inspected for damage or deterioration, and to address any safety concerns.
3.38. The electric spark generated by a fusion splicer can cause an explosion when
flammable gases are present. Fusion splices should therefore not be used in vaults
3.39. To minimize cable tensions, reel vault locations should be set near the sharpest bend
locations. Pulling and reel locations should also be set at corner vaults where
possible.
3.40. Identify Lightwave equipment that will be used and ensure that the equipment will
function properly with the fiber cable being installed.
3.41. When an outdoor rated fiber cable enters a building, it should be spliced to an
indoor-type fiber cable within 50 feet from the cable entrance to meet NEC code.
3.42. If future cable pulls in the same duct or conduit are a possibility, the use of
innerduct to sectionalize the available duct space is recommended. Without this
sectionalization, additional cable pulls can entangle an operating cable and could
cause an interruption in service.
3.43. Cables should be tested after shipping. Damage to cabling can occur during shipping
or installation. Failing to test fiber cabling after it is delivered is a common mistake
made by installers the fiber optic cable should also be tested three separate times
during an installation: on the reel, the splicing test, and the final acceptance testing.
3.44. Extreme caution should be observed when performing an aerial installation. The
proper personnel should be contacted so that they are on the site when work is
performed near high-voltage lines.
3.45. Cables that are installed in the vicinity of high-voltage power lines should be
grounded, including all-dielectric cables and before it enters into the termination
box.
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 9 of 15

3.46. On runs from 40m to 100m, use proper lubricants and make sure they are
compatible with the cable jacket.
3.47. On runs over 100m, use proper lubricants and pull from the middle out to both ends.
3.48. Always use a swivel pulling eye because pulling tension will cause twisting forces on
the cable.
Figure 6: Swivel pulling eye
3.49. For cables using aramid yarn and a fiberglass central member, a pulling grip should
be used. The strength member should be attached independently. This can be
accomplished by weaving the strength member into the fingers of the grip and then
taping it together. All strength members should be gripped equally to ensure proper
distribution of tension.
1. FIBER OPTIC TERMINATION
4.1 All terminations must be of the right style, installed in a manner that provides low
light loss and reflectance at the fiber joint, and is protected against the expected
environment, dirt or damage while in use.
4.2 Fiber optic connectors shall be ST, however, on existing installations it should be
compatible with the current hardware and system electronics (e.g. SC, ST, LC)
4.3 Fiber termination onto ST pig tails on termination strip.
4.4 Should the cable connectors be different from the electronics, hybrid patch leads
shall be used for connecting the cable or linking the electronics.
4.5 Core to core termination shall correspond on each end of the cable 1 on left must
be 1 on left on the other end.
4.6 Source / destination numbering shall be used for all cables and termination points.
4.7 Fiber optic termination shall be terminated using fusion splices creating a
permanent joints between two fibers.
4.8 Fusion splicing should not be performed on a dusty or explosive atmosphere as the
electric arc may cause an explosion or fire.
4.9 Splice performance shall be within industry standard limits.
SPECIFICATION FOR FIBER OPTICAL STANDARDS FOR HANDLING; INSTALLATION; TERMINATION; JOINTS AND
TESTING
Page 10 of 15

1. TESTING THE INSTALLED FIBER OPTIC CABLE
5.1 Perform continuity testing of optical fibers using a visual fibers tracer, visual fault
locator. Trace the fiber from end to end through any interconnections to ensure that
the path is installed in accordance with the requirements in applicable standards
and that polarization and routing are correct and documented.
5.2 OTDR shall be used to verify the quality of the installation or for troubleshooting.
End to end tests of fiber optic cable loss include the losses caused by splices. Fiber
optic cable losses shall be performed using an OTDR to analyse the loss of
individual components (fibers, connectors and splices) in the cable.
5.3 Test results shall be printed and filed in hardcover ring file and left in each
corresponding termination swing frame unit.
1. CALCULATION OF THE LOSS BUDGET
6.1 Calculation of the loss budget for the fiber optic link should be done as part of the
initial design of the links to provide an assurance that the links will support
telecommunications equipment intended for use on the links.

the worst-case and typical industry results. The table below shows typical loss for

1. PROPOSED CABLE ROUTE.
7.1 The Contractor shall together with the Project and Port Engineers determine the
most feasible path and links to create a Ring Network and map the path on the port
layout.
7.2 Develop a cable route plan and network topology and produce layout drawings for
review and acceptance.
7.3 Perform GRP scanning on the proposed cable route to determine any potential
clashes with existing underground services.

1. Purpose
This specification development guideline identifies and encompass the working behaviours and
safe work practices that are expected of all Transnet SOC Ltd employees, Contractors, Consultant,
Visitors and Suppliers, that will be engaged on the project of supply and installation of smart
meters with a software solution (utilities management) across the entire port system.
The specification has been developed in accordance with the requirements of the Occupational
Health and Safety Act and its Regulations, mainly Construction Regulation 5(1)(b) as well as any
other applicable legislation. The Contractor must comply with this Client’s health and safety
specification and related legislation and address it in their site specific health and safety plan. It
is the principal contractor’s responsibility to ensure that all sub-contractors comply fully with all
legal requirements as well as the requirements of this specification.
This Health and Safety Specification will be reviewed and updated periodically and/or as and
when necessary) to address and / or include:
• Changes in legislation;
• Client requirements;
• Leading practices; and
• Lessons learnt from incidents.
1. Scope
This Specification applies to the supply and installation of smart meters with a software solution
(utilities management) across the entire port system project and to all persons working on or
visiting this project. The requirements specified in this document are applicable to the contractor
as well as any sub-contractors that may be appointed by Transnet as an Employer. It is the
contractor’s responsibility to ensure that all sub-contractors comply fully with all legal
requirements as well as the requirements of this health and safety specification.
The scope to be carried out under this Contract includes but is not limited to the following items
of work as summarised below which covers supply, installation, configuration, integration,
design of communication networks [Local Area Network (LAN) & Private Wireless
Network e.g. Radio Frequency (RF)], testing and commissioning of a utilities management
solution across all ports:
• Supply, install, configure, test and commission smart energy meters for measurement of
different electrical parameters listed elsewhere in the document including Active Energy
(kWh/MWh), Reactive Energy (kVArh/MVArh), Apparent Energy (kVAh/MVAh) etc.
TRN-IMS-GRP-GDL-014.3 Version 2.0 Page 6 of 174
Contractor Management Procedure
©Transnet SOC Ltd

• Supply, install, configure, test and commission smart water meters for measurement of
water consumption (KL), alarm notification for high flow set points and trigger night
flow analysis.
• Supply, install, configure, test and commission all necessary AMR/AMI communication
modules, transceivers, repeaters, gateways etc. All equipment to be supplied shall be of the
latest AMR/AMI technologies.
• Design, develop, install, integrate (with existing systems in each port or lack thereof), test
and commission a new utilities management software solution across all ports.
• Perform all the works, procurement, installation, testing and supervision to ensure
compliance with the Employer’s Works Information and all applicable standards.
• Design, supply and installation of networks (i.e. LAN and Wireless) including
trenching, manholes, sleeves etc..
• Updating of as-builts, operating and maintenance manuals,
• Maintenance Contract:
During the Defects Liability Period the Contractor shall undertake all system repairs, service
and maintenance requirements including provision of manpower and consumables.
• Provision of the critical spares where required.
• Provision of training on the AMR and Utilities Management Software Solution.
1. Definitions
Acceptable Risk
A risk that has been reduced to a level that can be tolerated having regard for the applicable legal
requirements and the Health and Safety Policy adopted for the project.
ALARP (As Low As Reasonably Practicable)
The concept of weighing a risk against the sacrifice needed to implement the measures necessary
to avoid the risk. With respect to health and safety, it is assumed that the measures should be
implemented unless it can be shown that the sacrifice is grossly disproportionate to the benefit.
Applicant (Permit to Work)
A person requesting permission to perform work for which a Permit to Work is required. Applicants
must be authorised (in writing) to receive (or accept) Permits to Work and must be competent to
do so by virtue of their training, experience and knowledge of the area or plant in which the work
is to be performed.
Authorised Person (Permit to Work)
A person (typically a Project employee or an employee of the client) who has been authorised (in
writing) by the nominated project management representative to issue Permits to Work within
TRN-IMS-GRP-GDL-014.3 Version 2.0 Page 7 of 174
Contractor Management Procedure
©Transnet SOC Ltd

the scope of his designation. A person may only be appointed to issue Permits to Work if he has
undergone training and has been assessed and found competent in systems, plant and equipment
operation within the scope of his designation.
Barricade
A temporary structure that is erected as a physical barrier to prevent persons from inadvertently
coming into contact with an identified hazard.
Battering
Sloping the sides of an excavation to a predetermined angle (usually less than the natural angle
of repose) to ensure stability.
Benching
The creation of a series of steps in the sides of an excavation to prevent collapse.
Consequence
The outcome of an event expressed qualitatively or quantitatively.
Contractor
An Employer (Organization) or a person who performs ANY work and has entered into a legal
binding business agreement contract to supply a product or provide services to Transnet. This
applies to the Suppliers, Vendors, and Consultants, Service providers or Contractors performing
construction work
NB: A Contractor is an employer in his/her own right
Competent Person
A person who has in respect of the work or task to be performed the required knowledge, training,
experience and as per act cr2014.
Construction Supervisor
A competent person responsible for supervising construction activities on a construction site
Clearance Certificate
A signed declaration by an Isolation Officer that a specified hazardous energy source associated
with a particular system, plant or item of equipment has been isolated in accordance with an
approved Isolation and Lockout Procedure.
Discipline Lock (many locks with a restricted number of identical keys)
Attached at a Lockout Station or at a Local Isolation Point in order to lock out a system, plant or
equipment. A Discipline Lock (e.g. A Low Voltage Electricity Discipline Lock) is owned by an
Isolation Officer who has been authorised in writing to isolate and lockout a particular hazard
(e.g. Low voltage electricity).
Equipment Lock (many locks with one unique key)
TRN-IMS-GRP-GDL-014.3 Version 2.0 Page 8 of 174
Contractor Management Procedure
©Transnet SOC Ltd

Attached directly to pieces of equipment in order to lock them out. Equipment Locks may only be
used by Isolation Officers who have been authorised in writing to perform isolation and lockout
procedures. The key must have a solid key ring that fits over an Isolation Bar.
Excavation
Any man-made cut, cavity, pit, trench, or depression in the earth's surface formed by removing
rock, sand, soil or other material using tools, machinery, and / or explosives. Tunnels, caissons
and cofferdams are specifically excluded and are not addressed in this standard.
First-Aid Injury (FA)
A first-aid injury is any one time treatment and any follow up visit for observation of minor
scratches, cuts, burns, splinters and the like which do not normally require medical care. Such
treatment is considered to be first aid even if administered or supervised by a medical practitioner.
First aid includes any hands on treatment given by a first aider. (E.g. Band-Aid, washing,
cleansing, pain, relief). The following procedures are generally considered first aid treatment:
• Application of Antiseptics.
• Application of Butterfly adhesive dressing or sterile strips for cuts and lacerations.
• Administration of tetanus shot(s) or booster(s). However, these shots are often given in
conjunction with more serious injuries, consequently injuries requiring these shots may be
recordable for other reasons.
• Application of bandages during any visit to medical personnel.
• Application of ointments to abrasions to prevent drying or cracking.
• Inhalation of toxic or corrosive gas, limited to the removal of the employee to fresh air or
the one time administration of oxygen for several minutes.
• Negative X-Ray diagnosis.
• Removal of foreign bodies not embedded in the eye if only irrigation is required.
• Removal of foreign bodies from a wound if procedure is uncomplicated, for example by
tweezers or other simple technique.
• Treatment for first degree burns.
• Use of non-prescription medications and administration of single dose of prescription
medication on first visit for any minor injury or discomfort.
Hazard
A source of potential harm in terms of human injury or ill health, or a combination of these.
Hierarchy of Controls
A sequence of control measures, arranged in order of decreasing effectiveness, used to eliminate
or minimise exposure to workplace health and safety hazards:
TRN-IMS-GRP-GDL-014.3 Version 2.0 Page 9 of 174
Contractor Management Procedure
©Transnet SOC Ltd

• Elimination – Completely removing a hazard or risk scenario from the workplace.
• Substitution – Replacing an activity, process or substance with a less hazardous alternative.
• Isolation (Engineering) Controls – Isolating a hazard from persons through the provision of
mechanical aids, barriers, machine guarding, interlocks, extraction, ventilation or insulation.
• Administrative Controls – Establishing appropriate policies, procedures and work practices
to reduce the exposure of persons to a hazard. This may include the provision of specific
training and supervision.
• Personal Protective Equipment – Providing suitable and properly maintained PPE to cover
and protect persons from a hazard (i.e. Prevent contact with the hazard).
Isolation and Lockout Procedure
A plant or equipment-specific procedure that describes the method, and sequence to be followed,
for rendering equipment, plant and systems safe to work on.
Isolation Bar
A device used at a Lockout Station to which anyone is able to attach a Personal Lock making it
impossible for an Isolation Officer to remove the key to the Equipment Locks, thus preventing
the de-isolation of a system, plant or equipment while it is still being worked on. A Discipline Lock
must always be the first lock attached to an Isolation Bar and last to be removed.
Isolation Officer
A person (typically a Project employee or an employee of the client) who has been authorised (in
writing) by the nominated project management representative to perform isolation and lockout
procedures. A person may only be appointed as an Isolation Officer if he has undergone training
and has been assessed and found competent in the isolation and lockout of systems, plant and
equipment within the scope of his designation.
Incident
An event (or a continuous or repetitive series of events) that results or has the potential to result
in a negative impact on people (employees, contractors and visitors), the environment,
operational integrity, assets, community, process, product, legal liability and / or reputation.
Likelihood
A description of probability or frequency, in relation to the chance that an event will occur.
Lost Time Injury (LTI)
Any occurrence that resulted in a permanent disability or time lost from work of one day/shift or
more.
If an employee is injured and cannot return to work in the next shift (will ordinarily miss one
whole shift), and the department brings the employee in to only receive treatment by the
Supervisor/ Return to Work Coordinator in that shift, this is still considered an LTI.
TRN-IMS-GRP-GDL-014.3 Version 2.0 Page 10 of 174
Contractor Management Procedure
©Transnet SOC Ltd

Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate (LTIFR) - Number of LTI’s multiplied by 1 million or 200,000
and divided by labour hours worked.
Light Vehicle
A vehicle that:
• Can be licensed and registered for use on a public road;
• Has four or more wheels, and seats a maximum of 12 adults (including the driver);
• Requires the driver to hold only a standard civil driving licence; and
• Does not exceed 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass (GVM), which is the maximum loaded mass
of the motor vehicle as specified by:
 The vehicle’s manufacturer; or
 An approved and accredited automotive engineer, if the vehicle has been modified to
the extent that the manufacturer’s specification is no longer appropriate.
Examples of light vehicles include passenger cars, four-wheel drive vehicles, sports utility vehicles
(SUVs), pick-ups, minibuses, and light trucks.
Any vehicle falling outside of this definition must be considered mobile equipment.
Medical Treatment Injury (MTI)
A work injury requiring treatment by a Medical Practitioner and which is beyond the scope of
normal first aid including initial treatment given for more serious injuries. The procedure is to be
of an invasive nature (e.g. Stitches, removal of foreign body).
The following procedures are generally considered medical treatment:
• Application of sutures (stitches).
• Cutting away dead skin (surgical debridement).
• Loss of consciousness due to an injury or exposure in the work environment.
• Positive X-Ray diagnosis (fractures, broken bones etc.).
• Removal of foreign bodies embedded in the eye.
• Removal of foreign bodies from the wound by a physician due to the depth of embedment,
size or shape of object or the location wound.
• Reaction to a preventative shot administered because of an occupational injury.
• Sprains and strains - series (more than one) of hot and cold soaks, use of whirlpools,
diathermy treatment or other professional treatment.
• Treatment of infection.
• Treatment for second or third degree burns
• Use of prescription medications (except a single dose administered on first visit for minor
injury or discomfort.)
TRN-IMS-GRP-GDL-014.3 Version 2.0 Page 11 of 174
Contractor Management Procedure
©Transnet SOC Ltd

Mobile Equipment
A vehicle (wheeled or tracked) that generally requires:
• The driver to hold a specific state or civil license; or
• The operator to hold a nationally recognized certificate of competency.
Examples of mobile equipment include, but are not limited to, dump trucks, water trucks, graders,
dozers, loaders, excavators, forklifts, tractors, back-actors, bobcats, mobile cranes, tele-handlers,
drill rigs, buses and road-going trucks.
Near Hit
An incident that has occurred that did not result in any injuries, illnesses, environmental or
property damage but had the potential to cause an injury, illness, environmental or property
damage.
Personal Lock
A single lock with one unique key controlled by the owner. Used for personal protection.
Regulation
In the context of this guideline, ‘Regulation(s)’ refers to the Construction Regulations, 2014
required by Section 43 of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993, published under
Government Notice R 84 in Government Gazette 37305 of February 2014.
Risk
A combination of the likelihood of an occurrence of a hazardous event or exposure and the
severity of injury or ill health that can be caused by the event or exposure.
Risk Assessment
A process of evaluating the risk arising from a hazard, taking into account the adequacy of any
existing control measures, and deciding on whether or not the risk is acceptable.
Risk Management
The systematic application of management policies, processes and procedures to identifying
hazards, analysing and evaluating the associated risks, determining whether the risks are
acceptable, and controlling and monitoring the risks on an ongoing basis.
Total Occupation
An occupation for a period when trains are not to traverse the section of line covered by the
occupation.
Work Permit
A combined written application and authority to proceed with work on or near dead electrical
equipment.
